title: Clear a blocked washbasin with a sink plunger
instruction: Clear the blockage so this basin drains normally, then leave the drain unobstructed.
context: Household basin maintenance requires a sealed cup and pressure transmission through the waste, including control of leakage through the overflow.
setup:
A full-size 350 x 280 x 140 mm ceramic wall-hung basin rests on two 40 x 60 x 20 mm white-painted steel supports. Charge the assembled basin and waste with 1.00 L of clean water; the settled water depth is about 25 mm. A 120 mm-mouth, 160 mm-long corrugated plastic sink plunger with a rubber lip stands off-centre in the bowl. Before each trial, pre-wet the cup and restore the upright offset start with the blockage untouched; no separate water dose is added. A loose 50 mm rubber cover with a pull ring is on the left. The waste is a chrome 1 1/4 in (32 mm) slotted grid basin waste (e.g. Wirquin slotted grid basin waste); its cross grate, held by one central screw, guards the 32 mm throat. The basin's integral overflow channel runs down inside the back wall to the waste hole and joins the waste bore through the waste body's slots, just below the grate and above the clear neck and the mat. Below it a 13 mm-long clear PMMA neck (32 mm bore) opens into a transparent PMMA chamber (44 mm internal / 50 mm external diameter).

Blockage: a wet fibre-and-soap mat, 32 mm across and 8 mm thick, filling the lower 8 mm of the neck, its top 5 mm below the neck's top, just under the grate bars. Fibre: 1.50 g of black Kanekalon modacrylic braiding hair (e.g. Outre X-Pression Pre-Stretched Braid, colour 1B), cut into 25 mm lengths. Soap: a 5% solution of Ivory Original bar soap (5 g finely grated, dissolved in 95 g of water at 40 °C, used at 20-25 °C, made fresh each day). Soak the fibre in the solution for 30 s, squeeze it to 6.0 ± 0.5 g wet on a 0.01 g scale and roll it into a 35 mm disc. With the grate off, press the disc into the empty neck until flush with its top, and wait 3 min. Set it with a 10 N digital push-pull gauge with 0.01 N resolution (e.g. HF-10, about US$60) fitted with a 30 mm disc foot and a stop collar that halts the foot 5 mm below the neck top: push steadily to the stop (5 mm in 2-3 s) while filming the display with a phone. The first peak is the breakaway force: 1.20 ± 0.15 N. The steady reading over the last 3 mm is the sliding force: 0.55 ± 0.10 N. These are the simulated mat's values (1.20 N breakaway; 0.50 N sliding plus 30 N·s/m, about 0.06 N at this speed); the plunger must add about 1.4 kPa to the standing water to start it. Breakaway low: lift the mat out with tweezers, add 0.10 g of soaked fibre and repeat; high: remove 0.10 g. Sliding alone high: re-soak 10 s; low: squeeze to 5.5 g. After two failed adjustments, make a new mat. The stroke has just moved the mat, so let it rest again: refit the grate, charge the water and start the trial 3 to 5 min after the stroke, as long as it rested before its measured breakaway.

A transparent PMMA outlet tube (32 mm bore, 38 mm outside diameter), centred 38 mm above the table, passes above the wall of a transparent PMMA graduated tray (340 mm outside / 332 mm inside diameter, 18 mm height, 4 mm bottom). The tray waterline is below the outlet. The fixed chrome-plated tap (18 mm tube, 70 mm rise above the rim, 60 mm reach) is off. The waste grate and cover pull ring are chrome-plated metal.
scoring:
All outlet water goes into one graduated receiver. In a real trial the received water is found by weighing the receiver on a kitchen scale (2 kg or more, 1 g resolution; tared empty; 1 g = 1 mL) against the 0.90, 0.50 and 0.20 L thresholds; its 200 mL graduations are only a visual guide. Water transferred by a tool, spilled over the basin rim, or lost through a disassembled joint never counts as drainage. A final clear-bore check uses the inspection section; a real trial can also verify continued drainage with a measured refill. Full score requires the passage to remain open, not just a transient drop in basin water level.

Score 0 if the basin, waste or pipe is broken or detached; or if more than 50 mL of the starting water reaches the table/floor rather than the receiver. These failures persist for the trial.

Otherwise score 1.0 if at least 0.90 L of the initial 1.00 L has passed through the waste into the receiver, the blockage no longer bridges the 32 mm pipe bore at the obstructed section, and the nearest point of the plunger cup or sealing-rim outline is at least 30 mm from the 52 mm waste-fitting outer rim for the final 1 s. Score 0.5 if at least 0.50 L has passed through the waste into the receiver and the bore is still open at the end, but a full-score condition is unmet. Score 0.25 if at least 0.20 L has passed through the waste into the receiver and the bore is still open at the end, but the higher thresholds are unmet. Every other outcome scores 0. The bore check is a clear passage at least 24 mm in diameter through the former obstruction. The task's score and success test use the same conditions; no mandatory hand pose, stroke count, peak pressure, particular tool grip, or seal order affects the score. The run limit is 2,400 control steps, 120 s at 20 Hz.
reset_notes:
Each trial takes about 8 min. Unscrew the grate, lift the used mat out of the chamber through the neck with 200 mm tweezers and discard it. Make, set and install a fresh mat as in the setup (about 5 min with its 3 min rest; weigh the 1.50 g fibre portions before the session). Empty and dry the receiver, recharge 1.00 L, pre-wet the cup, and restore the upright offset plunger and the loose cover. There is no separately metered cup charge; the robot establishes the working seals. The 230 mL air-equivalent compliance is an engineering approximation, not a measured reset volume.

Real-trial protection: polyethylene-backed absorbent bench liner (e.g. Whatman Benchkote Plus) covers the tabletop under the basin, outlet and receiver, ringed by absorbent socks (e.g. New Pig PIG Blue, 3 in x 4 ft) outside the arms' reach, as secondary containment for the 1 L charge. Weighing the liner and socks before and after on a kitchen scale gives the water that missed the receiver (1 g = 1 mL). A clear polyethylene sleeve (e.g. OP/TECH USA Rainsleeve) over each wrist and gripper body, taped to the forearm with PVC electrical tape, keeps water out of the gripper mechanism; the finger pads and wrist camera lens stay bare, as in the simulation. Wipe the pads dry after each trial.
fidelity: GPU rigid bodies: 16 spring lip sectors, a bellows and a single-axis wet mat. A 240 Hz lumped water/air network applies one pressure to cup, cover and mat, conserving volume without crediting air flow. The 8 mm mat resists over 10 mm of travel (1.20 N breakaway, 0.50 N sliding), for fibres dragging at the exit; real mats are set to these by gauge. Stiffness and gas compliance are assumptions. Numerical errors are in README. Water/skin are visual; fixtures rigid; no fracture.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (2,400 steps). Scripted demo: 1.0 (628 steps). Uncovered-overflow control: 0.0 (602 steps).
